Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is made in a language, it can lead to inconsistencies in how words related to these objects are represented in word models. This study investigates whether the gender association for inanimate objects in languages that use grammatical gender is reflected in word models. To this end, we examine whether the similarity between the representations of inanimate objects and nouns for a specific gender are higher than those between the representations of inanimate objects and nouns for the other gender. Our analysis of the French and Italian languages, as well as that of a multilingual word model that was trained without any language-specific guidance, reveals that the similarity is indeed greater for the same gender. Conversely, we do not find any significant difference in similarity for languages that do not use grammatical gender, namely, English and Chinese. We explore the concept of stiffness in the context of time-invariant measures for systems governed by deterministic dynamics. In random maps, this concept is relatively well understood and is characterized by a specific type of exponential convergence. However, in the case of chaotic dynamical systems, such as smooth maps or flows, random stiffness loses its intuitive meaning. Instead, we consider a scaled version of it, focusing on its asymptotic behavior as a specific parameter approaches zero. We establish a method for detecting the stiffness of particular phases in systems with smooth dynamics and apply it to study the properties of certain Taylor series expansions. This approach also facilitates the analysis of stochastic bifurcations in systems governed by random maps and flows. Our method is particularly useful in the study of random frequency bifurcations in systems with partial hyperbolicity, where it helps us to establish the existence of randomly stiff stationary phases under relatively weak conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate its utility in the study of random stochastic bifurcations in systems with a finite number of random variables without requiring any assumptions about the system's hyperbolicity. In the case of random differential equations, this involves relaxing certain conditions necessary for the existence of randomly stiff periodic orbits. We also observe that our findings are consistent with the existing theory in the case of randomly stiff systems. In addition to these applications, we develop a novel approach to study the asymptotic behavior of the phase space expansions of systems governed by smooth maps and flows. This is achieved by using a specific type of average that is distinct from the traditional ergodic averaging technique. We establish that our averaging method is valid for a broader range of parameters than the traditional approach and is also less sensitive to perturbations in the system's parameters. Our approach, called Zero-Shot Pose (ZSP), enables pose estimation for novel objects without any training examples from domain-specific objects, relying on a single model. We create a unified representation for objects and their poses through a single neural network. We also introduce a novel method to generate pseudo training data based on the object's shape and its predicted pose, enhancing our model's performance. Our experiments on the LinePoseNet and COCO-Plus datasets show significant improvements in predicting key object features and pose interrelations. ZSP outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by 9% and 5% respectively on the LinePoseNet dataset. We also demonstrate ZSP's capabilities on datasets with objects that have never been seen before, achieving a mean keypoint accuracy of 62.2% which surpasses previous methods by 10%. Predicting short-term traffic is a crucial issue for intelligent transportation systems. This paper presents an enhanced traffic state prediction model called Trafic, which integrates multiple key attributes like speed, flow, and road conditions into a single framework. The Trafic model leverages a graph-based structure to capture relationships between road segments and incorporates spatial-temporal correlations. To address the challenge of limited sample data, the research proposes an innovative solution involving a dual-layered attention-based approach within a graph attention network. The Trafic model achieves superior performance in predicting traffic conditions with errors significantly lower than current best methods. The source code for Trafic is freely accessible on the GitHub platform at the specified URL. We investigate optimal methods for distinguishing between a pure state and another pure state in a complete quantum system. Initially, we demonstrate that achieving optimal success rates is feasible by developing adaptive strategies that alter only when the corresponding probability amplitudes change signs. Building on this, we find that such optimal methods can be represented by a unique, symmetric form involving the original states and specific, unique vectors derived from the reduced quantum system. Furthermore, we derive a formula to calculate the optimal success probability for any given initial state and provide a key condition for achieving 100% optimal success rate. Our research also extends to the scenario of discriminating between multi-particle states. Ultimately, we find that while generally, optimal success rates are only 50%, it is possible to reach 100% optimal success rate under certain conditions by employing online strategies, even in complex multi-particle systems. In certain cases, we show that the optimal strategies are as straightforward as measuring the entanglement with a specific partner. Our research may have significant implications for improving quantum key distribution and other applications. To confirm our findings, we present experimental results demonstrating the realization of 100% optimal success rates in various systems, including photons, ions, and atoms. Our research paves the way for the efficient use of quantum resources in practical applications. Recent studies have found signs in cosmic microwave background data suggesting the presence of a random gravitational wave background, possibly originating from violent first-order phase transitions in the early Universe. We investigate whether these predictions are supported by the properties of early Universe scalar condensates that are expected to drive such phase transitions. Light field technology is gaining popularity for its ability to capture detailed scene information and enable novel viewing experiences, all while maintaining spatial and angular resolution without the need for costly hardware. However, the inherent complexity of light field data management, stemming from its high-dimensional nature, has led to the development of various data compression techniques over the years. This paper provides a thorough overview of these compression methods, specifically focusing on interrelated topics such as light field acquisition, processing, transmission, and application areas. Furthermore, we offer a comprehensive analysis of existing light field compression techniques, discussing their relevant standards, research advancements, and future directions. To facilitate future breakthroughs, we also outline the key challenges that the next generation of light field compression algorithms should address. Finally, we offer suggestions on how to effectively present and publish light field technology to the broader image and video compression community. Our ultimate goal is to inspire future research in light field compression by identifying the most critical challenges and presenting standardization opportunities in this field. For cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two primary frameworks 
exist: the generic one, applicable to any language, and the one tailored to 
particular languages. In our research, we concentrate on the generic 
framework, specifically transfer learning methods involving multilingual 
encoders. We address a key issue with these methods: the need for extensive 
training data in the target language, often unavailable. To resolve this, we 
propose a data augmentation strategy that employs parallel corpora and 
back-translation. This approach trains a model to map texts from one language to 
another, allowing the creation of more examples for the multilingual encoder. 
Our experiments, conducted on the XQuAD and MLQA datasets, demonstrate that our 
technique significantly boosts the number of trainable parameters for each 
target language and, consequently, improves results. Notably, when combining our 
method with knowledge distillation, we achieve zero-shot or low-data 
cross-lingual results, rivaling results obtained with extensive target-language 
training data. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/soxito/xf.

In demographic research, various inverse probability weighting approaches are used for policy evaluations, focusing on the average causal effect of a particular variable across the population. However, current methods are limited in their ability to account for sampling designs when estimating population-level effects. This limitation becomes particularly problematic in public health policy interventions, where stratified sampling and estimation techniques are frequently employed. This paper presents a weighted local average and bias function that can be directly influenced by the sample size in each stratum, enabling the capture of population-level effects. We demonstrate the theoretical validity of this approach and provide simulation results showing that our estimation of the population average causal effect is remarkably accurate, with little to no loss compared to the theoretical gold standard. This method has been successfully applied to a real-world study examining the effects of smoking on mortality across 18 strata within the Finnish population. Our analysis reveals a notable negative effect of smoking on mortality across the entire population, with varying effects between strata. This highlights the potential of our approach to provide a more nuanced understanding of the average causal effect in complex demographic studies. Additionally, our research suggests that the average effect of smoking on mortality would have been considered negative only in strata with a high percentage of non-smokers. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes are hindered by atmospheric distortion, mainly due to varying refractive index caused by differential atmospheric temperature variations. This distortion is more pronounced for shorter wavelengths and greater altitudes, leading to chromatic effects that can be modeled as a wavelength-dependent dispersion. To mitigate the impact of this dispersion, Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors are employed to compensate for the observed star's apparent shift as it appears at various altitudes across different colors. This paper introduces a novel approach of using a learned neural filter to directly eliminate atmospheric dispersion in real-time, eliminating the need for prior spectroscopic data and enabling the correction to be performed in a single image processing step. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in reducing dispersion, particularly for observations conducted at high altitudes, and showcase its ability to combine multiple astrophysical phenomena, such as detecting variable stars within a single image. This method has been successfully implemented in a Raspberry Pi-based ADC system and verified to operate within 0.2 arcseconds of accuracy under real-world observing conditions. This breakthrough has the potential to be scaled up to larger ADC systems and integrated into telescope control systems, paving the way for widespread adoption in a variety of astronomical applications. We explore a concept called baryogenesis within a theoretical framework known as the $\Lambda\text{CDM}$ model, which includes four fundamental components: ordinary matter, dark matter, ordinary radiation, and a smooth dark energy component. We assume that dark matter has interactions with ordinary matter that are strong enough to influence baryon asymmetry, which would require the presence of matter that can decay into electrons and neutrinos. Since neutrinos are known to be fermions, we consider the possibility of dark matter being composed of fermions as well, which would allow for the creation of anti-dark matter through the process of antibaryogenesis. We examine the antibaryonic matter's decay into stable particles, which would not violate any principles of the fundamental theory of quantum general relativity and the electroweak theory. We also investigate the antibaryonic matter's interaction with dark matter, which would allow for the creation of matter-antimatter pairs, and subsequently, the decay of antibaryonic matter into particles that contribute to the matter-antimatter imbalance. We analyze the process of antibaryogenesis in detail, which would require the presence of matter that can decay into stable particles at temperatures corresponding to the mass of this matter. We also consider the constraints imposed by the Sakharov conditions, which would require the presence of CP-violation within the dark sector. In this study, we investigate Toeplitz algebras of specific types of functions on complex numbers and planes. These include translation-invariant subalgebras of bounded, uniformly continuous functions and those that include the Dirac delta function. Building on prior work by Arveson in 2006, we establish that such Toeplitz algebras are operator algebras complete with preduals, with particular classifications when the predual is separable. Additionally, we demonstrate that Toeplitz algebras related to the Dirac delta function are not finite-dimensional even in low dimensions. Furthermore, we show that certain Toeplitz algebras related to translation-invariant functions on the complex plane have well-defined limits as the scaling factor tends to infinity, mimicking the behavior of the Fourier transform. These limits can be expressed as closed subalgebras of bounded uniformly continuous functions on the complex plane, with similar results applicable to functions on higher-dimensional complex spaces. Object detection has been a prominent concern in computer vision, and recent advancements have led to impressive performance achievements. The emergence of knowledge distillation methods has significantly improved detection quality by sharing knowledge between models, however, current distillation techniques have several limitations. Firstly, they are model-dependent and can only facilitate knowledge transfer between similar architectures. Furthermore, they are prone to over-reliance on the teacher model's features, hindering the distillated student model's ability to adapt to open-set detection tasks. To address these challenges, our research introduces Open Distillation to boost zero-shot detection capabilities. Open Distilation is an innovative framework that enables knowledge transfer across detection models of varying complexities from different families by leveraging their shared semantic features. The method utilizes a semantic feature extractor to align the semantic spaces of the detection models, allowing for effective knowledge transfer. The results demonstrate that Open Distilation can successfully distill features from complex to simple models, achieving notable performance enhancements in zero-shot detection for models without pre-existing labels. The findings also indicate that our approach can effectively transfer knowledge across models with distinct feature representations, such as Faster-RCNN and non-detection models. The proposed method has the potential to unlock new applications for object detection models, including those that were previously infeasible. The code and models will be made publicly available. The paper includes a new benchmark that showcases the potential of Open Distilation, highlighting its ability to unlock new detection capabilities for models initially designed for standard multi-class classification. The benchmark includes a new dataset called OpenVOC, comprising object categories not present in PASCAL VOC 2007, including objects like a fork, a chair, and a person wearing glasses. The results show that models distilled with Open Distilation can successfully detect these novel categories, achieving a significant 10.5% increase in mean average precision (mAP) compared to baseline models. The results of the Open Distilation method will be made publicly available for evaluation purposes. Despite numerous studies, there is still no comprehensive review of the existing research on this topic. This paper investigates the effectiveness of iterative pruning strategies on the interaction between layers in complex neural networks. To this end, it frames the network pruning process as an optimization problem that seeks to minimize the network's size, subject to constraints on the intra-network (similar to a Gaussian process) and inter-network (independent) covariance. It is observed that single-stage pruning techniques produce sub-networks with distinct structural properties. In contrast, our experiments show that an iterative two-stage approach, first optimizing intra-network and then inter-network structure, yields better generalization performance. Notably, the surviving sub-networks often exhibit a more compact and localized structure within each layer, while the inter-network connections are more sparse and randomly distributed. Our findings suggest that the specific structure of the sub-networks itself may not be crucial for improved performance, but rather the controlled interaction with neighboring neurons. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the efficacy of the pruned sub-networks largely depends on the specific type of data used for training. Overall, our research indicates that network pruning can be a valuable tool for understanding neural network behavior, especially when used in conjunction with optimization-based techniques to manipulate the network's structure. Leveraging the newly found connection, this work proves that a key invariant associated with it exhibits Picard-Fuchs differential equations, a crucial discovery that facilitates a detailed topological examination of the moduli space. Utilizing these equations, this work further demonstrates that the connection's curvature is a well-defined class over a specific relative space, providing an alternative perspective on the moduli space. This finding is then applied to derive an expression for the connection's curvature in terms of Schottky-Gotzmann weights, a set of invariants characterizing the curve's properties. Ultimately, this work shows that the connection's curvature is a constant that does not rely on the choice of connection, a result that holds over the entire moduli space. A comparison with existing results for curves of low genus or genus zero shows that the constant's value in these cases aligns with previously established values. This research aims to address this issue by developing new, transparent categorization methods based on tree models that provide clear explanations for their results. These methods are crucial in auditing, as they allow for a thorough examination of each data point's contribution to the final outcome. According to our study, the trade-off between explaining the results and maintaining fairness is not as significant as previously thought. By testing these methods on real-world audit data, we found that they are nearly as effective as more complex machine learning models but require much less time and effort to analyze. Overall, our results indicate that these explainable tree models are a suitable option for use in auditing. Furthermore, our research also introduces a new approach for measuring fairness in auditing, known as fairness through adjustment, which can be used to adjust the weights of individual data points to maintain fairness while maintaining their predictive accuracy. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the lack of reliable deformation field ground truth for real-world deformable terrain. Current methods for generating ground truth rely on artificially created scenarios, such as making ground truth available only for specific gaits, or using simulated environments that don't reflect real-world conditions. We address this problem by developing a new framework for producing ground truth on actual deformable terrain before testing robotic locomotion on it. Our framework utilizes deep learning to predict ground deformation based on a single image of the terrain and evaluates its effectiveness through quantitative metrics such as peak displacement and displacement variance. We also present the first successful application of this framework to predict ground deformation under a robotic leg, demonstrating its potential for improving robotic locomotion on deformable terrain. Video recordings and source code for this research can be found at https://youtu.be/6b8B8b8B8B. Additionally, our code will be publicly available on https://github.com/your-branch/existing-repo.

To validate its effectiveness, we employed the YFCEB dataset and observed that our algorithm's output closely resembled that of the k-means algorithm using PCA dimensionality reduction. This implies that smaller feature sets and faster runtime can be achieved without compromising on clustering quality. Based on these results, we propose that this algorithm may have a significant impact in scenarios where data is scarce, resources are limited, and speed is a top priority. The frequency of these vibrations is within the conventional range found in plant and animal tissues and food. The measured shear moduli show a pronounced dependence on vibration amplitude, displaying an almost logarithmic increase with the vibration's acoustic intensity. The observed behavior can be attributed to an energy transfer mechanism from the ultrasonic field to the colloidal particles, causing them to move out of equilibrium and thereby reducing the gel's viscosity. The implications of our findings could lead to the development of new methods for controlling gel-like materials through ultrasonic means, potentially allowing for the in situ adjustment of gel properties. A key characteristic of CAP is the use of pairwise preferences. Researchers have focused on developing stable matching algorithms for different variants of CAP, with pairwise preferences being a crucial aspect. However, recent studies have shown that pairwise preferences can be efficiently converted into comprehensive lists of preferences using polynomial complexity, without affecting the stability of matching algorithms. As a result, pairwise preferences and the associated list-based approaches share many commonalities. Furthermore, several scenarios utilize partial or incomplete preference lists, and some settings even impose constraints on preference lists to ensure stability. Given the significant impact of preference list characteristics on the performance of matching algorithms, researchers have explored various strategies to minimize the impact of preference list construction on computational resources. Notably, using short and concise preference lists has gained popularity in some domains, as seen in the context of distributed stable matching algorithms. A recent study has even established the existence of instances with minimal and unique preference list configurations for all potential matchings. A key contribution of this study lies in the development of new proof techniques, specifically a novel graph-theoretic approach to establishing short preference list properties in the context of distributed stable matching algorithms. Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are limited in their ability to comprehensive measure summary quality, focusing primarily on coherence and relevance. We introduce the SummScore metric, which assesses summaries across four key dimensions: 1) fluency; 2) secretion (relevance); 3) comprehension (understanding); and 3) originality (novelty). The metric utilizes a multi-task learning approach, combining four separate scores derived from language models, and weights them according to their individual reliability. The evaluation of SummScore on seven datasets reveals it outperforms existing metrics in a majority of cases, and when fine-tuned on a specific dataset, it surpasses the performance of these traditional evaluation methods. Notably, SummScore demonstrates more nuanced performance in evaluating summaries generated by abstractive models compared to traditional metrics. The code and pre-trained models are available on GitHub. In future research, we aim to enhance SummScore's performance by incorporating additional language models and expanding its training datasets. The ultimate goal is for SummScore to facilitate the development of more accurate and informative summarization models. The conventional approach to 3D object detection, which relies on LiDAR data, can be inefficient and unreliable in certain situations such as low lighting conditions or physical obstructions. In response to these limitations, we introduce a novel camera-based method for 3D object detection, which utilizes point cloud data derived from auto-focused video frames to achieve high levels of accuracy. Our proposed framework, known as CAM3DNet, is designed to enhance both efficiency and precision by leveraging a multi-scale point representation that incorporates depth information. Specifically, we utilize a 2D feature extractor to obtain initial point features, which are then refined and aggregated across multiple scales via a point aggregation network. Our framework also incorporates a point loss function that minimizes the distance between aggregated points and ground truth points, which further improves precision. Extensive evaluations conducted on the KITTI object detection benchmark demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing LiDAR-based and camera-based approaches, with results showing significant improvements in mean average precision (mAP) for multiple object size categories. Notably, CAM3DNet is capable of achieving high levels of reliability and efficiency, with processing times of 0.04 seconds or less for input video frames. Our accompanying code and model weights are available for public access on the GitLab platform. Ultimately, our research reveals that high-quality camera data can be an effective substitute for LiDAR data in 3D object detection, particularly when combined with a well-designed feature extraction framework. Our findings also highlight the potential for further accuracy gains through the incorporation of additional sensor modalities, such as RGB data. Our research further investigates the use of LiDAR data in a fusion-based approach, where we demonstrate that a simple late-fusion strategy can yield substantial improvements in mAP for small objects without compromising overall processing times. Our research code and model weights are available for public access on the GitLab platform. Our research contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) a novel camera-based method for 3D object detection, (2) a new point aggregation loss function, (3) a new framework known as CAM3DNet, (4) a new fusion strategy for combining camera and LiDAR data. Our research findings reveal that high-quality camera data can be an effective substitute for LiDAR data in 3D object detection, with results showing significant improvements in mAP for multiple object size categories. Our research demonstrates that a simple late-fusion strategy can yield substantial gains in mAP for small objects without increasing processing times.

This paper presents a novel stream processing framework designed for big data clusters based on micro-services. Unlike traditional monolithic approaches, our framework decomposes stream processing functions into independent, scalable micro-services. The framework's core components, including input parsing, data processing, and output aggregation, are distributed as micro-services to facilitate seamless scaling and resource allocation. We implemented a prototype, SPIM, which outperforms Apache Flink in both efficiency and adaptability, as illustrated by experiments using a cluster and varied workloads. SPIM achieves these gains through a stateless execution model, stateless recovery mechanisms, and a micro-service scheduler enabling flexible resource allocation and operator distribution. Notably, SPIM's performance benefits from a near-optimal micro-service scheduling strategy known as HBS, which prioritizes high-throughput and efficient resource usage. Evaluation shows SPIM's micro-service scheduler boasts a 2.5x improvement over optimal parallelization methods and 1.5x over other scheduling methods, while SPIM as a whole surpasses Apache Flink in execution speed and scalability. For instance, SPIM processes TPC-DS queries 2.3x faster than Apache Flink when configured for 16 parallel operators and a cluster with 20 nodes. Furthermore, SPIM maintains its performance under workload fluctuations, whereas Apache Flink struggles to scale and maintain consistency under dynamic workloads. Overall, our framework provides a novel approach to stream processing, empowering users to tailor stream processing functions to specific applications, scale stream processing operators, and achieve resource efficiency in micro-services. As a result, applications can now seamlessly integrate with external services, as the stream processing pipeline can be easily reconfigured to adapt to changing requirements. Future research directions are outlined in Section 7. The source code for our framework is publicly available at https://github.com/utdcs-labs/spim. A live demo of SPIM can be accessed at https://live.utdcs-labs.org/spim. The experimental results and data used in this paper are available at https://utdcs-labs.org/spim/expresults. The investigation considers the single-lepton final state with the most favorable production mechanisms and highest available luminosity, 139 inverse femtobarns. The most effective search strategy involves analyzing the single-lepton events with the highest transverse momentum and at least one b-jet, employing a multivariate analysis to enhance sensitivity. The most promising combination of variables yields a limit on the single-lepton cross-section of 0.26 pb at 95% confidence level, with the most effective variable being the total jet mass. Voice assistant applications such as Alexa and Google Assistant rely on semantic parsing to convert natural language inputs into machine-readable representations. Current state-of-the-art techniques for semantic parsing, particularly in the context of dataset SPARQL, have resulted in a significant performance gap when compared to human abilities. This limitation is largely due to the complexity and resource-intensive nature of deep learning models required for high-performance semantic parsing. However, such models often struggle with adaptability and portability, particularly on lower-resource devices. To address this challenge, a new approach known as LightSPARQL has been developed to achieve state-of-the-art performance using lightweight models and a novel data augmentation strategy that leverages the capabilities of logic-based query rewriting. This approach not only achieves superior results on the SPARQL dataset but also demonstrates improved efficiency, with a significant reduction in computational and memory requirements. Notably, experiments indicate that LightSPARQL can run at least 4 times faster on lower-resource GPUs while using 6 times less memory compared to the leading deep learning models. The existence of Zeeman spectroscopy on board the BRETHE instrument allows for the precise determination of magnetic field strengths in the atmospheres of cool stars. A comprehensive review of the primary objectives, technological advancements, and initial findings of the BRETHE mission are presented. A notable outcome from its first year of operation is the collection of a vast dataset of 123 spectra. Analyzing these spectra revealed magnetic fields in 93 stars, with a significant majority of field measurements in the range of 100-1000 Gauss. As the data show, magnetic fields decrease substantially with increasing altitude above 2.5 gauge, or approximately 6 kilopascals. Moreover, the distribution of field strengths is skewed towards lower values below 1000 Gauss in the majority of stars. A notable finding is the presence of strong magnetic fields in the young, rapidly rotating M-type dwarf DX Cancri, with a field strength of approximately 1.2 kilogauss. A detailed analysis of the magnetic field's spatial distribution across the star's disk reveals a field strength of about 1000 Gauss at the center and diminishing as one approaches the disk's edge, where it reaches a field strength of about 300 Gauss. By utilizing computational models, the absorption behavior of the thin silicon films was examined under normal incidence and compared to alternative metal-based reflectors. Results showed that a photonic band gap spacer could elevate the absorption of charge carriers within the thin layer by 15%, and even surpass the performance of an ideal dielectric spacer, due to resonant enhancement of absorption under specific conditions. These findings underscore the value of considering multi-scale interactions between electronic states, photon modes, and crystal structure in designing innovative thin-film solar technologies. Moreover, the study highlights the feasibility of achieving improved solar energy conversion with relatively simple thin-film configurations, rather than relying on intricate and expensive nanostructures. Ultimately, the study's predictions suggest that thin-film solar cells with a photonic band gap crystal could achieve higher efficiency compared to standard metal-backed counterparts, with potential gains of up to 0.5% in efficiency. This implies that a photonic band gap crystal could be an effective and cost-effective alternative to conventional metal reflectors in thin-film solar technology. Notably, the study's findings are highly relevant to a wide range of thin-film solar technologies beyond silicon, and could be applied to systems utilizing alternative semiconductor materials. We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB. Compared to previous models, our approach shows improved accuracy by approximately 1.5 dB. To assess its practical applicability, we apply the model to optimize and design 4D formats with a constant power constraint via sequential convex programming. To facilitate format optimization, we introduce a novel representation of the nonlinear interference that can be computed efficiently using Monte Carlo simulations and depends only on the last two stages of the transmission system. Our results demonstrate the potential for substantial spectral and power gains with optimized 4D formats. Specifically, for a given spectral efficiency of 7 bits/s/Hz, we found that our optimized formats can achieve up to a 4.5 dB increase in performance compared to commercially available polarisation-division multiplexing systems. Moreover, we derived the optimal 4D format that maximizes spectral efficiency at 7 bits/s/Hz, enabling the extraction of its underlying structure. Our analysis shows that the optimal format employs a single peak in the amplitude spectrum located at the end of the transmission span, accompanied by a minimal number of secondary peaks. This characteristic allows for the development of a closed-form approximation of the nonlinear interference, potentially facilitating the design of even better 4D formats. In addition, we investigated the relationship between the optimal 4D format and the interference patterns produced by different types of nonlinearities, varying degrees of polarization, and coupling between signals within the transmission span. Our results are presented in a graphical format, enabling the design of 4D formats tailored to specific system conditions at a given spectral efficiency. For instance, for 4.5 dB gains, we identified a set of optimal formats suitable for systems with moderate level of polarization mode dispersion and significant cross-talk between signals. Conversely, for systems with minimal cross-talk and polarization mode dispersion, we found that the optimal 4D format exhibits a symmetric pattern with two equidistant peaks located along the transmission span. This analysis highlights the potential for substantial performance improvements in polarisation-division multiplexing systems through the design of optimal 4D formats. However, when different segments of the matrix are subject to distinct levels of noise, this adaptive weighting strategy becomes impractical. This work proposes a new formulation for such a situation, drawing on the 'cycle sparsity' concept in magnetic resonance imaging to ensure robustness by adjusting the penalty for rank constraints. We support our approach with numerical analyses and extensive numerical experiments that demonstrate its advantages. We also derive a certificate of optimality for the proposed method and establish its relationship with other existing methods through numerical results. Additionally, we illustrate its potential in solving real-world problems in image and matrix recovery. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence that our approach can be viewed as a form of 'cycle denoising' when applied to partially observed data in a controlled environment. We also provide a theoretical guarantee for the accuracy of the recovered matrix under certain conditions. Finally, we provide a computational complexity assessment for the proposed method and suggest possible future research directions. We introduce a cutting-edge diagnostic framework that utilizes a BERT model to identify COVID-19 infections in lung CT images in conjunction with clinical data. The framework incorporates transfer learning and adapter techniques to fine-tune BERT for extracting distinct features from both visual and textual sources. To assess visual-bert representation capabilities, we conducted an experiment with COVID19-BERT and found it to be on par with pre-trained ImageNet models. We evaluated the fine-tuned model on two datasets and observed that it achieved an impressive 89% accuracy when applied to real-world clinical scenarios. Notably, our study demonstrates that BERT can effectively integrate and combine the strengths of both modalities to produce robust diagnostic results. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that specific visual features extracted by COVID19-Bert are indicative of viral distribution, bronchitis, and ground-glass-hypertension, while textual inputs inform the model of patient symptoms, age, temperature, and treatment. As a result, our proposed approach can provide a more comprehensive understanding of COVID-19 disease mechanisms. With further refinement and validation, this diagnostic framework has the potential to be adapted for use in smart hospitals and healthcare systems. This paper presents a comprehensive benchmark of speech learning, focusing on the impact of various task-related and non-task-related audio inputs. Eight self-supervised models are evaluated, incorporating different modalities like speech, noise, music, child sounds, and mixtures. Six speech tasks are assessed to track performance regression after removing speech signals. Our experiments on 16 datasets across 11 languages demonstrate that a single, universal model can achieve comparable results to language-specific models, requiring only language labels for initialization. This finding suggests a promising approach to universal speech learning across languages. Notably, our results show that a well-designed model can perform competitively on downstream speech tasks despite being trained on non-speech inputs. This is an unexpected outcome, given the inherent differences between speech and other modalities. Our study aims to provide a foundation for future research on speech learning, enabling the development of more efficient and versatile models that can accommodate various types of audio inputs. Our code and models will be publicly available to facilitate future research. This study focuses on the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the basic three-dimensional fermion system on a one-dimensional lattice. The paper demonstrates how the Cartan generator's action is represented as a difference matrix, and subsequent algebraic constructions yield invariant polynomials with respect to this action. These polynomials serve as wave functions for the corresponding quantum numbers within the system. By utilizing these polynomials, various properties and relationships between multiple independent conserved quantities can be derived. Notably, the study reveals a connection between the conserved quantities and the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-Whittaker functions. Additionally, the paper explores the invariance of the fermion system under the action of the raising generator and introduces a framework for classifying the resulting degeneracies. This classification is achieved through the study of a generalized parabolic Schubert variety within the Poincaré polynomial of the general linear group's Weyl chamber wall. Utilizing the classification, degeneracy patterns can be explicitly calculated for various symmetry levels. The findings are further validated through the derivation of Bethe vector-based expectations, which are in agreement with existing results for non-distinguished observables. Lastly, the study examines the symmetry action of the raising generator and outlines an approach to constructing multiple independent conserved quantities for general observables within the system. This involves establishing a correspondence between the conserved quantities and the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-Whittaker functions for a decorated loop group associated with its maximal torus. Utilizing the conserved quantities, expectations of observables can be computed via the Bethe vector-based approach. The study also provides a generalization of the Gaudin Bethe ansatz for multiple conserved quantities and outlines a framework for constructing Bethe ansatz solutions for general observables within the system. The findings are further validated through the derivation of explicit degeneracy patterns for multiple conserved quantities. The paper concludes by examining the symmetry action of the raising generator within the fermion system in the presence of twisted boundary conditions and a non-symmetric Hamiltonian. In this context, the study introduces a decorated generalization of the affine Weyl group associated with the torus of the twisted affine Kummer generator and utilizes it to derive multiple independent conserved quantities. The study also generalizes the Bethe vector-based approach to this setting and provides a novel solution to the twisted Bethe ansatz equations for multiple conserved quantities.

This paper presents a comprehensive study on 3D object localization in complex urban settings using only a single point position fix derived from GPS and DGNSS signals. We provide an in-depth analysis of several key challenges: accurately estimating the 3D position of an object, the impact of significant position errors on localized objects, and the reliability of object localization in urban areas. We propose a straightforward yet robust mathematical framework for estimating a 3D object's position from a singular measurement. We also introduce a novel method for calculating the position error vector of a localized object and develop a statistical model to assess the reliability of object localization. Our research is based on real-world urban data obtained from GPS receivers with a singular antenna configuration. We demonstrate that object localization can be effectively achieved with minimal hardware setup. Furthermore, our results reveal that the proposed approach yields reliable and robust 3D object localization in urban settings. This study has significant implications for diverse applications, including those that utilize GPS-based metadata and 3D object localization for object tracking and surveillance. To facilitate the reproduction of our findings, our code and data are freely available on GitHub. This allows for the evaluation of our proposed approach using various GPS data sets and is easily adaptable to diverse scenarios. Our research is entirely based on publicly accessible data sources, ensuring reproducibility and transparency. Our proposed approach is versatile and can be applied to various applications with distinct parameters. We anticipate that our research will inspire further work on object localization in settings where diverse viewpoints are present. Our study is the first to provide a comprehensive solution to this problem and is expected to contribute to the broader literature on machine learning and computer vision. The dataset employed in this study is derived from the BMTI Berlin dataset, which is accessible at the following address: https://www.beuth-hochschule-berlin.de/de/forschung/forschungsdaten/Berlin-Motion-Times-Index. As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified requirements into formal specifications to ensure reliable software development. This goal is challenging on a larger scale due to the inherent subjectivity of requirements, which are often difficult to clearly define. Our solution, CitySpec, is a natural-language processing assistant designed to facilitate this process for city-based services by translating informal specifications into formal ISO 20022 message definitions. CitySpec integrates multiple components, including text analysis and formalization tools, an extensive knowledge database, and an intuitive interface for user guidance. To correct inaccuracies in quantum circuit computations, we've introduced an error mitigation strategy that exploits the properties of hidden variables. This method determines error probabilities by simulating the behavior of small-scale errors and their effects on multiple circuits. The model utilizes a set of hidden variables that are randomly assigned to simulate the behavior of physical qubits. Since these variables can represent complex error patterns, we've developed an expectation-maximization algorithm to calculate the probability distributions of errors for a given gate basis through iterative calculations. The results show that using this model, we can accurately predict the behavior of larger gates by combining the effects of smaller gates. The efficiency of this approach is characterized by its computational cost, which increases linearly in relation to the number of gates. The effectiveness of this model is demonstrated by comparing it to more traditional error mitigation strategies, such as repeated measurements and the density matrix renormalization group method, in a variational quantum eigensolver application. The findings indicate that our approach outperforms and surpasses current methods, providing a reliable basis for predictions and paving the way for the development of more sophisticated error mitigation strategies. Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is investigated in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis of storm events reveals a significant negative correlation between wind speed and wave height during intense weather conditions, with the strength of this correlation increasing as the severity of the storm increases. Based on this findings, new models of extreme weather are developed, taking into account the varying relationship between wind and wave data to provide more accurate predictions. By applying these models to future climate scenarios, an increase in the severity of storms is detected, with more extreme weather events expected to occur at a rate 10-20% higher than current forecasts. This research demonstrates the benefits of combining data from different sources and considering the complexities of extreme weather events. By leveraging data from satellites, historical records, and advanced climate models, a more nuanced understanding of future climate risks can be achieved, leading to improved decision-making and resource allocation. In the last few years, research has focused on shifting strategies for the eigenvalues of nonsymmetric matrices, leading to various methods such as matrix balancing, which is an important step in analyzing dynamical systems, computing clusters in multidimensional data, and more. These methods aim to relocate the eigenvalues of a given matrix A by adding a shift matrix B, resulting in a new matrix B+A. Balancing is defined by the condition that the eigenvalues of the shifted matrix B+A lie on specific lines in the complex plane. While matrix balancing has been extensively studied for real symmetric matrices, its analysis for nonsymmetric matrices remains underdeveloped. This paper extends the matrix balancing framework to a broader theory called elliptic operator shifting, which encompasses a diverse set of shifting methods beyond balancing. This new framework is based on a specific condition that defines the possible directions in which eigenvalues can move under the transformation E → T(E) = T0 + E, where T0 is a given matrix and T is a linear transformation. This condition leads to the definition of an elliptic operator as a matrix that preserves the direction of eigenvalues when applied to an appropriate subspace. These operators are used to characterize the behavior of matrix functions and to determine whether certain matrices can be connected to their transformed counterparts through a continuous path of matrix evolutions. This concept is used to extend the matrix balancing framework to a broader one, which applies to general matrix transformations. This paper also explores the applications of elliptic operator shifting in analyzing the behavior of matrix functions, as well as its connections to other related problems. Specifically, it demonstrates that balancing is a special case of elliptic operator shifting involving a rotation by 45 degrees, and it discusses how this framework can be used to compute clusters in multidimensional data, to analyze dynamical systems, and to compute B-spline surface patches. Additionally, it discusses the challenges associated with finding a path between two matrices that differ by a small transformation and the limitations imposed by the matrix's rank and size. Finally, it suggests potential research directions and applications of elliptic operator shifting. The growing interest in transparent AI has led to a surge in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have gained popularity for their flexibility in handling complex recommendations. However, current post-hoc explanations often prioritize comprehensibility over transparency and trustworthiness, which are essential for users. To address this, a new approach is proposed, incorporating a theoretical framework of user experience to systematically evaluate the essential attributes of explainable recommendations. This leads to the introduction of a user-centric metric, referred to as Quality of Explanation (QoE), which aims to enhance user satisfaction through clear and trustworthy recommendations. By reformulating the recommendation made by a black-box model into a pairwise set of items, a novel algorithm is designed to optimize QoE in the long run. Experimental results on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm in enhancing user experience in comparison to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, a user study validates the proposed approach by showing that users prefer explanations generated by the proposed algorithm over those produced by current techniques. This research contributes to the development of user-centric explainable recommendation systems by introducing a novel metric and algorithm that prioritize transparency and trustworthiness. The proposed metric can be applied to various explainable recommendation methods to enhance their user-friendliness. Future research directions are also outlined in the conclusion. In this note, we outline a more extensive proof that establishes the contraction of a broader class of rankine-hugoniot discontinuities, including those related to shocks and contact discontinuities, in systems satisfying the Lipschitz condition. The proof relies on the notion of metrically compatible solutions and employs a dynamic regularization technique. The result has implications for the stability of solutions to conservation laws, including bounded solutions. The proof's approach is similar to a previous study by Cancelier and Vialard, although our result is specifically tailored to address an open question raised by Bressan regarding the stability of contact discontinuities. The result is also applicable to solutions with Lipschitz perturbations of discontinuities. The proof's details are presented in a series of annexes that provide additional mathematical insights. Annex A discusses the well-posedness of solutions to conservation laws in the context of the Wasserstein distance, while Annex B explores the notion of metrically compatible solutions. Annex C provides a comprehensive review of the necessary functional inequalities, while Annex D presents the main technical result of Canc\`elier and Vialard regarding the stability of rankine-hugoniot discontinuities. Finally, Annex E outlines the proof of the main theorem in detail. The study is a part of a broader research effort aimed at developing a comprehensive theory of solution stability for conservation laws. This study proposes a new framework for classifying toxic comments in a fully automated setting, taking into account comments that are incomplete, ambiguous, or generated randomly. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to achieve ensemble generalization by training multiple sub-networks within a single master model.  Despite being inefficient in terms of parameter usage, as it essentially amounts to using an ensemble of duplicate models, MIMO offers better predictive outcomes and lower training costs compared to single-column networks.  In an effort to address this resource wastefulness, we introduce a new method called MOLO, which involves using a master module to combine multiple optimization-based sub-networks.  Through the application of an alternating optimization technique, MOLO allows for the identification of diverse sub-networks, thereby avoiding the need for excessive model duplication.  Our theoretical findings indicate that MOLO is capable of achieving MIMO's enhanced ensemble generalization performance, while also reducing the overall number of model evaluations.  Experimental results from both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the efficacy of our proposed method in producing strong generalization with significantly fewer model evaluations.  Notably, MOLO outperforms MIMO across a variety of test datasets and evaluation metrics.  Moreover, an analysis of the learned sub-networks reveals distinct areas of expertise within each, thereby offering valuable insights for further optimization.  Our code is freely accessible via the following link: https://github.com/ashishramesh/MOLO.  Finally, an ablation study examining the impact of incorporating auxiliary information on image classification is presented in the accompanying paper.  The findings suggest that auxiliary information can be beneficial, but only if properly utilized; otherwise, it may introduce unnecessary distractions and have a negative impact on performance.  The study also reveals that auxiliary information can be an effective tool for data augmentation when used in conjunction with ensemble methods.  Notably, incorporating auxiliary information can result in a significant boost in predictive accuracy, exceeding 10% in certain cases.  The findings of this study are presented in detail within the paper.  The source code is freely accessible via the following link: https://github.com/ashishramesh/MOLO. Past and potential future climates can be categorized into three main regimes, each with distinct characteristics, including a stable regime with moderate precipitation, an arid regime with extremely dry conditions, and an anaemic regime with reduced water availability due to slow atmospheric water circulation. However, research suggests that there are limitations to using simple two-dimensional climate models to study regimes, particularly when it comes to understanding complex water cycles. To better understand the dynamics of regimes, researchers have developed a new approach that uses a simplified model to study the stability of idealized climate states and their transitions into different regimes. The results show that the simple model can accurately replicate the stability of both stable and arid regimes, and it reveals that the boundary between the stable and arid regimes is highly responsive to even minor changes in CO2 levels, leading to potential catastrophic shifts into these regimes as the Earth's climate continues to warm. Furthermore, the simple model has revealed new insights into the characteristics of extremely warm 'hothouse' climates, including the rapid turnover of water between the atmosphere and the oceans, which may lead to the development of new methods for studying these extreme climate states. The research also highlights the importance of considering the stability of equilibrium states and the possibility of transitions into both arid and hothouse regimes under future climate change scenarios. The findings of this study have significant implications for our understanding of climate change and the potential for complex and extreme climate states to develop in the future. This study presents a novel approach to detecting Hindi and Bengali hate speech, which poses significant challenges due to the limited availability of labeled datasets and the dynamic nature of language slang. To overcome these obstacles, we propose an innovative data augmentation technique that utilizes cross-lingual transfer, combining translations with linguistic patterns to create synthetic labeled data. Additionally, we suggest a two-part classification model, integrating a multilayered CNN-BiLSTM architecture with a self-supervised pre-trained language model to capture nuanced context. Our experiments, which involved the evaluation of eight different models on two newly created labeled datasets, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, yielding an 81.1% macro F1 score in Hindi and an 80.5% macro F1 score in Bengali. Notably, our approach outperformed a leading baseline in both languages and achieved comparable results to the state-of-the-art in English hate speech classification, highlighting its potential for broader applications across multiple languages. This paper addresses the challenge of unseen scene text instances in Optical Character Recognition (OCR). Current OCR models rely on extensive amounts of annotated data, which is often not feasible to obtain. Our proposed Transcription by Association (TBAA) method enables an OCR model to translate image contents into text through self-supervised learning. This is achieved by introducing a significant semantic shift between an image's semantic representation and its corresponding transcription. Our experiments on the Scene Text 1-Billion-Chars and TotalText datasets have shown that TBAA yields comparable results to the current state-of-the-art models, all of which were initially designed for supervised learning. Furthermore, TBAA's self-supervised capabilities facilitate its ability to adapt to new languages without pre-existing models, as demonstrated on the TotalText dataset. Our findings indicate that TBAA's performance is largely influenced by the level of semantic shift introduced in the image-text discrepancy. Consequently, we have developed a new evaluation metric, referred to as Text Similarity (TexSi), to quantify the similarity between an image's predicted text and its actual meaning. This allows researchers to optimize the TBAA method by adjusting the text-generating objectives to produce more accurate text representations. Ultimately, our work highlights the feasibility of using self-supervised learning to tackle the unseen text problem without requiring pre-existing models. Our key method involves an innovative change of variables in complex integrals that express the L-functions as linear combinations of convolutions, allowing us to control the denominators of the algebraic components. Developing effective mobile robots that operate in unfamiliar environments poses a significant challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose an algorithm grounded in Reinforcement Learning that enables a robot to determine an optimal collision-avoidance strategy when interacting with other moving entities. Our approach involves training the robot within a simulated large-scale environment built on the Unity Engine and powered by the Bullet Physics Engine. Leveraging the Unity Machine Learning framework, we rapidly prototype and test multiple reinforcement learning configurations to achieve high-quality results in a computationally efficient manner. Furthermore, we validate the robustness of our solution in diverse, unseen scenarios to ensure its practical applicability in real-world scenarios. Our research demonstrates that a trained agent can successfully navigate through complex scenarios at least five times faster than one that employs traditional learning methods. Consequently, we believe that our approach has the potential to significantly accelerate future research in this area. The challenge is particularly pronounced when dealing with large datasets, where the limitations of traditional statistical methods necessitate the development of new approaches. The emergence of advanced data science tools, including deep learning and neural networks, has the potential to mitigate these complexities and unlock new insights into time series analysis. A significant shortcoming of current deep learning practices is the inadequate handling of uncertainty. The field of Bayesian deep learning offers alternatives to model uncertainty and irreducible prediction uncertainty. We propose an efficient method to quantify both types of uncertainty using a modular, multi-layer perceptron-based network, known as Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs), which can be trained alongside standard maximum likelihood procedures. By leveraging Hamiltonian mechanics, HNNs provide an explicit representation of the data distribution, allowing us to define a lower and upper bound for the predictive entropy. We demonstrate that the lower bound corresponds to the model uncertainty and the upper bound encompasses both model and irreducible uncertainty. We validate our approach by applying HNNs to synthetic and real-world datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR10, and chest X-ray images for pneumonia diagnosis, while comparing results with other state-of-the-art approaches in uncertainty quantification. The source code is publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/robustresearch/HNN. MuMuPy extends and enhances the capabilities of existing dimuonium interaction calculators, offering enhanced features, stability, and ease of use. MuMuPy is designed to be user-friendly, allowing researchers to easily obtain results for their specific needs. Additionally, it includes a comprehensive documentation and a set of educational materials to introduce students to quantum mechanics and muon physics. Using the functional approach, the rate of change in fermionic correlation functions due to interactions with a large number of low-energy bosonic modes is examined. A criterion is established for when the impact of these interactions can be neglected, and this is shown to be related to the relative strength of fermionic and bosonic gaps. Several examples, including a two-dimensional superconductor and a doped Mott insulator, are used to demonstrate how this criterion can be applied. These examples highlight the importance of both the density of states and the interaction strength between fermions and bosons in determining the stability of quasiparticle states. As a result, even at low temperatures quasiparticle states may not be fully developed in systems where the density of states is high and the interaction between fermions and bosons is weak. This is particularly relevant to the context of superconductivity in high-temperature superconductors, where the presence of spin excitations may impede the development of quasiparticle states. Our analysis also offers insight into the stability of quasiparticle states in the presence of strong electric currents, which may be exploited in the design of efficient superconducting nanocircuits. The findings presented here are relevant to a wide range of systems, from ultra-cold atom systems to solid-state systems, and could be verified via experimental measurements of the response function. As an alternative, even in the absence of direct experimental evidence, the stability of quasiparticle states can be evaluated through the analysis of transport properties, which may be controlled via interactions with low-energy bosonic modes. This paper presents an enhanced Retrieval Augment Generation (RAG) architecture,
implemented entirely within the Longformer framework, thereby making the
original RAG compatible with long-form text. To improve the RAG architecture,
we introduce an end-to-end architecture that integrates both retrieval and
generation stages. By training the entire network in sequence, our approach
enhances the interaction between these components and allows for a unified
end-to-end optimization. Evaluations on various datasets demonstrate the
superiority of our method over the existing RAG architecture, which uses the
same pre-trained Longformer model. Notably, our approach outperforms the
existing RAG architecture by a significant margin on datasets with longer
text passages. Moreover, our experiments show that an enlarged memory bank
further boosts the performance of our method. To facilitate future research,
we make our implementation available on GitHub under the name
`longformer-RAG`. Additionally, our implementation adheres to the original
training settings specified in the respective papers, which can be found on the
websites of the RAG and Longformer projects. Lastly, our results are
accompanied by an ablation study that examines the influence of various
parameters on our method's performance. To view the study, please visit

The effectiveness of crowdsourcing platforms in gathering high-quality human annotations depends on several factors, particularly how clearly instructions are provided and how tasks are designed. This research involves collecting annotations from a large group of workers for image retrieval, using a platform that allows us to control and adjust both aspects. We conducted a comprehensive study, collecting over 100,000 annotations from over 400 workers under different experimental conditions. We analyzed the quality of these annotations, using metrics relevant to machine learning tasks, and found significant effects of both instruction clarity and experiment setup on annotation quality. We also explored the characteristics of high-quality annotations, using a theoretical model to explain the variability of annotation quality and providing practical recommendations for improving task design. Finally, we evaluated the performance of image retrieval systems using these annotations, demonstrating the importance of selecting high-quality annotations and highlighting potential biases in annotation quality. Our research provides a foundation for future studies on crowdsourcing image retrieval, and our dataset and code are publicly available. This research aims to contribute to the understanding of crowdsourcing image retrieval, and our results are expected to be relevant for other image processing tasks as well. We plan to release our data and code publicly on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/2022M5MIR/IRCrowd. TS2-Net incorporates two key modules: the token shift module, which enables the translation of individual words, and the token aggregation module, which synthesizes the translated words to form a new sentence in the target language. This study investigates the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning to determine the position of a camera, specifically in dynamic and complex environments. We evaluated and compared the effectiveness of two widely employed methods: the iterative closest point (ICP) algorithm and direct minimal explicit solvers (DMES). To assess the accuracy of these methods, we created a comprehensive dataset derived from the well-established TUM RGB-D dataset. Our experiments involved simulating two scenarios: one with randomly generated ground truth poses and another without ground truth poses. The results showed that ICP is the most reliable method but also the most susceptible to noise and inaccurate when the initial guess is flawed. In contrast, DMES is more resilient to noise but less affected by imperfect initial guesses. Notably, both methods can benefit from the integration of additional data, such as object information. To address the limitations of these traditional techniques, we also propose a novel deep learning approach based on pointnet that can estimate camera poses. Although this approach performs well in terms of accuracy, it is also prone to errors when confronted with unexpected objects not included in the training data. Overall, our study provides a detailed analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of these camera pose estimation methods and sheds light on their potential applications in real-world robotics settings. For small treewidth graphs, vertices can be efficiently separated using O(1) memory, but this becomes challenging for larger graphs. This study focuses on the memory efficiency of vertex separator algorithms. It is demonstrated that under the Unique Games Conjecture (UGC), vertex separator algorithms necessitate at least Ω(2^treewidth) memory. Additionally, UGC implies that no vertex separator algorithm can accomplish the task in O(2^treewidth) memory without also increasing runtime exponentially with treewidth. However, by discarding the UGC assumption, a more optimistic scenario emerges: there exists a vertex separator algorithm that uses treewidth bits of memory while only requiring polynomial time. This result is achieved through an algorithm designed for tree-decomposable graphs, which utilizes O(treewidth) memory and runs in polynomial time. This algorithm can then be adapted for general graphs by first applying a tree-decomposability algorithm, followed by the specialized vertex separator. Consequently, while the overall runtime of the two-stage algorithm becomes exponential with treewidth, the memory usage remains treewidth bits. This study thus highlights the distinct trade-offs possible between memory and runtime in vertex separator problems. For linear bandit algorithms operating in dimensions where features scale at most quadratically with options, we analyze how the eigenvalues of the design matrix influence regret. The expected regret in such scenarios is shown to be directly proportional to the sum of the top eigenvalues when features are relatively sparse. Building on this finding, we outline a method to estimate these design matrix eigenvalues from empirical data and propose a technique to dimensionally reduce these matrices while preserving their most significant properties. The result is a simplified design matrix with improved in-sample prediction accuracy, achieved through a singular value decomposition of the design matrix and selecting the top eigenvalues for projection. We demonstrate the practical effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the Contextual Bandit problem and achieving a 25% decrease in test loss when using the dimensionally reduced design matrix, along with a 43% reduction in computation time. A fundamental assumption in active inference is that agents internalize their environment through Bayesian probabilistic models. While an excellent framework, its applicability is uncertain, particularly in biological systems. This paper explores a simplified scenario of a rod moving unpredictably across a circular path, and a frog-like creature attempting to accurately track its position using sensory input. Unlike active inference's premise, our approach does not rely on an agent-generated model of its environment. Instead, our results demonstrate that, in the absence of detailed environmental information, effective behavior can be achieved by adopting the most likely explanation for observed sensory inputs. This process, referred to as 'online learning,' allows the agent to adapt its behavior as it gathers more data. Notably, our findings reveal that, in the long term, the agent's behavior may converge towards an optimal solution similar to that predicted by active inference. This study highlights the potential for systems to develop adaptive and efficient behaviors in the absence of a pre-existing environmental model, and suggests that the active inference framework might be an optimal solution to a complex probabilistic problem. Our work also suggests that the observed adaptive behaviors in biological systems could be based on a simplified, non-Bayesian interpretation of active inference. This non-Bayesian approach relies on a fundamental distinction between learning about the world and learning about the most likely explanations for sensory inputs. Our results provide insights into the neural mechanisms that could underlie this adaptive behavior, and offer a new perspective on the complex interplay between sensory input, learning, and decision-making processes in biological systems. The accuracy of Automated Essay Scoring (AES) is a primary concern, and enhancing its long-term grammatical accuracy component (which assesses essays of up to 500 words) could significantly impact its overall performance. To address this, we developed a language model that integrates a memory mechanism to track and repeat the essay's structure, and evaluate its effectiveness in comparison to existing leading models through human evaluation and automated testing. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves improved performance in identifying grammatically correct essays, and achieves a higher agreement rate (94% or above) with human scorers, while also maintaining a high level of consistency in scores. Notably, our model's performance in identifying errors in essays is comparable to, and in some cases superior to, the performance of experienced human proofreaders in identifying minor errors, and achieves a higher overall performance in this task as well. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the knowledge knowledge taxonomy to identify areas where our model excels, and to pinpoint potential areas for further improvement. Overall, our results indicate that our approach is effective in improving the long-term grammatical accuracy component of AES systems. One of the most difficult aspects of applicable research, domain adaptive pedestrian detection, is adapting to new domains with significantly lower annotation requirements.  Current methods often rely on aligning feature distributions or estimating target domain labels from source annotations, but these may not adequately account for the complex domain shifts encountered in real-world scenarios.  In contrast, our approach tackles this problem by reformulating it as a multi-source multi-label learning issue.  Specifically, we introduce a new model called CM$^2$LAA, which incorporates multiple features from diverse sources to create an aggregated representation for the target domain.  By utilizing semantic correlations across sources to determine shared labels, our approach effectively reduces source diversity.  Additionally, our aggregation strategy allows for the suppression of source-specific features, thereby promoting target domain generalizability.  Experiments conducted on widely-used datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, with CM$^2$LAA yielding substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art benchmarks by as much as 8.4% AP.  Notably, our method outperforms many competitors despite operating without access to target domain annotations during training.  Specifically, our approach is comparable to other unsupervised domain adaptive methods, even when the target domain annotations are available.  Moreover, our approach allows for the identification of source-specific features and target domain labels, providing valuable insights into the relationship between these entities. This research focuses on generating high-quality audio from a lower-quality input by employing neural networks to pre-process and enhance the audio before upscaling it in quality. As consumer-grade music recordings are commonly affected by distortions like background noise, echo, and distortion due to compression, we use a pre-processing model to remove these imperfections before upscaling. Our experiments, which involved both real and synthetic audio data sets, demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in improving the audio upscaling process. Additionally, we showcase the benefits of our method in making neural networks more resilient to variations in audio tone and timbre. Furthermore, we successfully applied our approach to various types of audio upscaling, including individual instrument upscaling. Our pre-processing model is now being integrated as a pre-training strategy for neural networks to improve audio upscaling tasks. This research is expected to contribute to future advancements in audio upscaling technology. The code and audio data for this research are available online. Furthermore, a mobile app showcasing the effectiveness of our approach can be accessed through a mobile device. This research is supported by funding from the Brazilian government.
