The study of the two-dimensional Schrödinger operator $H_\lambda = -\Delta + q + \lambda V$ demonstrates that for small $\lambda > 0$, the solution $u$ of the exterior Dirichlet problem is uniquely determined by the value of $u$ on any subdomain with smooth $\Gamma$ and the restriction of $q$ and $V$ on $\Gamma$. This generalizes a 1997 result obtained by Mel'nikov and Simon. The key to this result is the application of two complex geometric optics constructions, one of which was developed by Lin, Burq, and Corti, and the other developed by Ikawa. The former is used to control high-frequency components of $u$ in certain directions, and the latter is used to control normal components. By combining these constructions, we can cover all directions, and by taking a linear combination, we can make $u$ independent of frequency modulation. The final step is to use this independence to control the reflection coefficient and complete the proof. The approach in this paper can also be used to prove the so-called four-ball inequality in a more straightforward way. Researchers aim to develop meta-learning methods that enable generalizable
adversarial training capabilities across various tasks and domains by
focusing on representation learning. A robust feature representation can
harness the benefits of adversarial training, although current methods have
limitations when applied to classification problems. This paper presents a new
new approach, Meta Representation Learning via adversarial training (MaRL),
which can be used for both classification and detection tasks. This method
utilizes a meta-learning framework to optimize a task-specific model, where
the backbone network, designed for general-purpose object detection, learns to
process representations that can effectively handle classification or
detection tasks after passing through task-specific adapters. Experimental
results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, which outperforms state-of-
the-art models on the CIFAR100 dataset in adversarial settings. Additionally,
our method achieves comparable performance to the top-ranked methods on the
ImageNet dataset in non-adv adversarial settings and significantly improves
robustness against strong adversarial perturbations compared to popular
classification models. MaRL's source code will be made available for public
use. This research aims to contribute positively to the field of AI by
investigating the potential of meta-learning and adversarial training to
improve the robustness and generalizability of deep neural networks. Furthermore,
our study highlights the importance of testing machine learning models in
adversarial settings to ensure their reliability in real-world applications. 
In line with the growing interest in AI for the greater good, this research
aspires to shed light on the complex interactions between adversarial training,
meta-learning, and domain generalization methods. Ultimately, this work seeks
to inspire further exploration of these fascinating yet intricate topics. 
Lastly, our method's ability to effectively handle classification tasks has
inspired a new approach for improving medical image classification tasks at

We propose a Knowledge Distillation strategy to transfer knowledge from high-performance, multilingual machine translation models to their lower-resource counterparts. This involves a target teacher model, which is initially pre-trained on multiple languages, including the resource-scarce language in question. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a temperature-scaled cross-attention mechanism within the teacher model. Importantly, the teacher model is trained in a fully parallel manner, eliminating the need for paired data and manual annotation. Consequently, it generates soft labels that capture its inherent knowledge. Subsequently, a student model, specifically a transformer-based encoder and decoder, is fine-tuned using these labels in conjunction with gold-standard data. Notably, the teacher model's knowledge is observed to be more effective in improving the resource-scarce student model's performance compared to leveraging multilingual knowledge from its pre-training data. Extensive experiments conducted on three low-resource languages - Khmer, Lus, and Sinhala - demonstrate the substantial gains achieved by our proposed distillation approach. A thorough error analysis further underscores the teacher model's ability to accurately predict words that are either rare or absent in the resource-abundant languages, thereby facilitating better performance. To validate the transfer learning mechanism, we also developed a set of artificially generated pseudopair data, which reveals that the teacher model's knowledge is indeed transferable and can be effectively utilized to improve the performance of lower-resource languages. Ultimately, the distillation strategy is observed to be a viable solution for machine translation in scenarios involving resource-scarce data. The research findings are made available through an open-source implementation on the HuggingFace Transformers and the Fairseq platforms. The pre-trained models used in this study can be accessed at the following repository location - https://github.com/ashwin-101/Transformer-Based-KD. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as n approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that such a limit exists and is continuous. The Turan density of any graph F can be expressed as a sum of the densities of its induced subgraphs G, by considering the maximum number of edges in an F-free but G-containing r-uniform graph on n vertices and dividing it by the total possible number of edges. The set of induced subgraphs of F that maximize this ratio is known as the extremal family of the Turan number. The rise of deep learning has significantly improved the accuracy of semantic segmentation tasks, but the success of such methods heavily relies on the availability of a large, well-labeled dataset. Given the high cost of manual labeling, developing efficient data augmentation techniques to minimize the requirement for labeled data is crucial. In the context of detecting pneumonia using chest X-ray semantic segmentation, we investigated various data augmentation methods and their combinations to identify the most effective approaches. Our experiments involved training models with and without augmentations on a dataset of real-world chest X-ray images, and the results showed that specific combinations of image transformations can effectively replace a substantial portion of the dataset, enabling accurate pneumonia detection with a reduced need for labeled data. Based on our findings, we recommend using a combination of dataset rotation, color normalization, and image cropping to achieve optimal performance, ultimately achieving a high accuracy of 0.97 using a minimal dataset of 50 labeled images when applying a 9-fold data augmentation strategy. The integration of artificial intelligence and traditional knowledge is crucial to address the significant unsolved problems in science and society. However, the current dominant paradigm of large-scale, high-complexity models may not be the best approach to leverage knowledge effectively. Overemphasizing model complexity can result in diminished capabilities for effective knowledge application and may hinder progress in this field. Conversely, a simpler approach that focuses on utilizing knowledge through linguistic means may provide more opportunities for innovation. This perspective discusses potential issues with current AI models and the benefits of adopting a simpler approach that utilizes text-based knowledge, highlighting the significance of this paradigm in AI development. This alternative approach is also explored in the context of existing work, with notable examples including text-based few-shot learning and large-scale multimodal language models. The potential of this paradigm is further demonstrated through the presentation of two case studies, one involving the integration of knowledge to enhance the visual quality of generated images and another involving the application of knowledge to improve the semantic accuracy of these images. The results show that the integration of knowledge can be effectively and efficiently achieved through text-based few-shot learning, with significant improvements in both semantic accuracy and visual quality. This research aims to inspire a more comprehensive reevaluation of the existing frameworks and methods in AI to strike a balance between harnessing knowledge and algorithmic complexity. We introduce the variational separability verifier (VSV), a novel method that uses variational quantum algorithms to determine whether a multi-qubit quantum state is entangled or exists solely as a product of separate single-qubit states. To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it is essential to enhance performance capabilities. This can be achieved by leveraging existing infrastructure and optimizing network configuration.  A promising approach is to develop a joint optimization method for both network configuration and function distribution. This method can be realized through a model called Partially Observable Markov Decision Process and subsequent reinforcement learning techniques.  This paper presents a novel method for optimizing WiFi networks, focusing on maximizing network utility as the primary goal.  Initially, the problem is defined as a POMDP challenge and solved using deep reinforcement learning, and the results demonstrate improved performance capabilities compared to traditional mesh networks.  Furthermore, the approach exhibits resilience during network disruptions, and the results scale well to accommodate an increasing number of nodes.  This method also offers flexibility in its application, allowing it to operate on a range of network architectures without modification.
